claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy contains significant internal stress and microstructural inhomogeneity.
Annealing for 10–120 minutes at 400–700 °C will partially crystallize the alloy.
Annealing reduces lattice strain and relieves residual stress.
Annealing improves microstructural or magnetic homogeneity.
Annealing refines the grain structure or grain boundaries.
Grain boundaries, lattice distortion, and residual-stress-related defects mediate magnetic domain-wall motion.
Relaxing residual stress and homogenizing the microstructure facilitates magnetic-domain rearrangement.
Annealing broadens and smooths the magnetostructural transition.
Partial crystallization stabilizes the first-order magnetostructural transition during low-field cycling.
Annealing reduces magnetic hysteresis during low-applied-field cycles.
Annealing lowers the coercive field.
The annealed alloy retains a magnetocaloric response and entropy-change magnitude similar to the as-deposited alloy.
The as-deposited baseline has a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with a large entropy change.
The as-deposited baseline has highly hysteretic entropy changes.
Internal stress and microstructural inhomogeneity limit heat exchange in the as-deposited state.
The predicted behavior applies to thin films or similarly processed samples annealed for 10–120 minutes at 400–700 °C.
The predicted behavior may differ for arc-melted ingots, melt-spun ribbons, or treatments outside the stated annealing window.
Compositional variation may influence the magnetocaloric and hysteretic outcome.
Reduced XRD peak FWHM can indicate reduced strain and changes in grain size after annealing.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as an ordered single-phase hexagonal crystal, while the intervention is described as partial crystallization without explaining what amorphous or uncrystallized fraction remains to crystallize.

The hypothesis attributes improvement to grain refinement, but reduced XRD FWHM after annealing is also consistent with grain growth; the cited evidence specifically says annealing decreases grain-size reduction rather than establishing refinement.
